input.question: Why do the lightbulbs inside my car seem to never burn out but I have to change the lightbulbs in my lamp at least once a year?
input.ground_truth: The light bulbs in your car stay on when you open the car door, and close afterwards. If it takes you ten seconds to get in or out of the car, and you do that ten times a day, that's 100 seconds a day. Over fifteen years, that's 547,500 seconds -- or 152 hours. A household incandescent bulb lasts for about 1,200 hours. A CFL for about 8,000 hours, and LEDs for about 25,000. TL;DR -- the lights in your car aren't on for nearly as long as the lamp in your living room.

Also, they don’t stay on all the time—they only turn on when you need them, like at night or when it’s dark. Because they are protected and not used all the time, they last a long, long time before they need to be changed.

Your lamp’s lightbulb is like a toy you play with every day. You turn on the lamp every night to read or see in the dark. That means the lamp’s lightbulb works a lot more than the ones in your car. Because it works so much, it uses up its “energy” faster and needs to be changed more often, like once a year.

So, the car’s lightbulbs last longer because they are protected and not used as much. The lamp’s lightbulb works harder and gets changed more often!
